1.pericope_label: And it came to pass in the fourth year of king Darius, that the word of the Lord came unto Zechariah in the fourth day of the ninth month, even in Chisleu; When they had sent unto the house of God Sherezer and Regem–melech, and their men, to pray before the Lord, And to speak unto the priests which were in the house of the Lord of hosts, and to the prophets, saying, Should I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done these so many years?

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gloss the errand as literally to stroke the face of the Lord, an expression for affectionate entreaty, and explain that the priests are called those belonging to the house of the Lord not because they served in the room of the firstborn, as one interpreter had argued, but simply as the men who by their mediatorial service could obtain an answer to a question put in prayer. Ellicott dates the mission to 518 before Christ, denies that the word Bethel is ever used of the temple, renders it that the people of Bethel sent Sherezer and Regemmelech, and traces the name Sherezer to Assyrian.

Gill places the mission near two years after the temple foundation was laid and near two years before it was finished; he notes that the Hebrew is singular, when he sent, reports a Jewish opinion that Bethel was a man's name, and insists against the others that the senders were the Jews already returned and settled in Judea, since the answer is directed to them throughout the chapter. Calvin agrees with Ellicott that the word is nowhere used for the temple and renders accordingly, its men rather than his men, and shall we weep rather than shall I weep.

Clarke supplies the calendar note, that the ninth month answers to part of November and December, and observes that the month-names appear only under and after the captivity; he takes the senders to be Jews sent by those who remained at Babylon to ask whether the fasts appointed at the destruction of the city were still binding. Wesley agrees that the enquirers were the captives still continuing in Babylon, and glosses the separating of the fast as a withdrawal from worldly cares and designs.

Henry measures the interval from the prophet's earlier visions at above two years and notes that he had not been idle in between but had preached no sermon then that was left on record. He leaves the question of the senders open, observing that the answer might be directed not to the messengers only but to all the people, and reads the enquiry as a readiness to continue the fast if God should so appoint, holding that a method of religious service found beneficial ought not to be altered without mature deliberation.

debates.question: What does the word Bethel mean here, and who sent the deputation?

positions.position: Not the temple: the people of Bethel sent Sherezer and Regemmelech, the town's name standing for its inhabitants.
The Hebrew is singular; a Jewish opinion made Bethel a man's name, and the ancient versions read it as a sending unto Bethel, meaning the city where the house of God was building.

debates.question: Were the enquirers the exiles still in Babylon or the returned Jews in Judea?

positions.position: The captives who still continued in Babylon.
The Jews already returned and settled in Judea, since the answer is directed to them throughout.
The question is left open; the answer might be directed not to the messengers only but to all the people.

outliers.claim: The priests are described as belonging to the house of the Lord not because they were appointed to serve there in the room of the firstborn, as Kliefoth argued, but simply as the persons who by their mediatorial service could obtain an answer to a question put in prayer.

4.pericope_label: Then came the word of the Lord of hosts unto me, saying, Speak unto all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years, did ye at all fast unto me, even to me? And when ye did eat, and when ye did drink, did not ye eat for yourselves, and drink for yourselves? Should ye not hear the words which the Lord hath cried by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and in prosperity, and the cities thereof round about her, when men inhabited the south and the plain? And the word of the Lord came unto Zechariah, saying, Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, saying, Execute true judgment, and shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother: And oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart.

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that the question, though asked by a few, concerned the whole nation, so the answer is given to all, and that the reply falls into four sections each opened by the formula that the word of the Lord of hosts came, a testimony that the prophet spoke not of himself; he counts the seventy years exactly from the killing of the governor left over the ruined city to the month of this embassy, recasts the seventh verse as a statement rather than a question, places the plain west of Judah, and corrects the grammar of the received version at the last clause. Keil and Delitzsch reject as strange the opinion that the prophet named in the eighth verse is an earlier man of that name living before the captivity.

Gill takes the people of the land as the men of Judea who sent the messengers and were represented by them, allows the eating and drinking to mean either common meals or festivals, and fills out who the protected are in the closing commandment: those with no husband and no parents to care for them, in a strange land and unable to help themselves.

Clarke gives the days of both fasts, notes that in Jewish usage the title of the former prophets belongs to the historical books while the writing prophets are the latter but judges that here the preachers before the exile are meant, takes the plain for the flat country about Jericho, and says the enquirers deplored the loss of the temple and its riches but never humbled themselves for the iniquities that caused it. Wesley puts the charge bluntly, that they pleased themselves and not God, weeping more for the inconvenience of their trouble than its sinfulness, and turns the seventh verse into an argument that observances which did not preserve the city in prosperity cannot profit them now.

Henry presses the doubled question hardest: that they are asked whether they fasted unto him, even to him, shows the weight laid on intention, there being the carcase of the duty but none of its life and power, and to fast and not fast to God is to mock him. On the eating and drinking he offers two readings and prefers the second, their common meals, self being the centre where the lines of all their actions met; and he notes that the duties then recited are not fasts and sacrifices but justice and mercy, binding by the light of nature apart from any prophet.

debates.question: How should the seventh verse be construed?

positions.position: Not as a question but as a statement, are not these the very words, with no verb needing to be supplied.
As the question it appears to be, and an argument: if such observances did not preserve the city in its prosperity they cannot profit them now.

debates.question: Where is the plain named alongside the south?

positions.position: The flat country about Jericho, the south being the wilderness and mountainous parts of Judea.

outliers.claim: If fasting does not quicken prayer, increase godly sorrow and alter the course of the life, it does not answer its own intention at all, however frequent, long or severe it may be.

11.pericope_label: But they refused to hearken, and pulled away the shoulder, and stopped their ears, that they should not hear. Yea, they made their hearts as an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the Lord of hosts hath sent in his spirit by the former prophets: therefore came a great wrath from the Lord of hosts. Therefore it is come to pass, that as he cried, and they would not hear; so they cried, and I would not hear, saith the Lord of hosts: But I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations whom they knew not. Thus the land was desolate after them, that no man passed through nor returned: for they laid the pleasant land desolate.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the phrase not pulled away but offered a stubborn shoulder, as an ox refusing the yoke; he takes the hard stone to be simply a very hard one and traces the English word, in its modern form diamond, to a Greek adjective meaning unconquerable first applied to steel, noting that the ancient Greek version dropped the figure and rendered it that they made the heart disobedient, and that the same version wrongly made the following clause future. Keil and Delitzsch render the two verses through and describe this second word as recalling the fathers' disobedience, and its consequence, for a warning.

Gill identifies the refusers as the Jews before the captivity and goes furthest of all on the hard stone, reporting the Jewish tradition that the thing meant is no stone but a creature the size of a barley corn, able to cut the hardest stones, used by the lawgiver in hewing the two tables and by the king in cutting stone for the temple, and unbreakable by iron; from which he draws that as naturalists say the adamant is softened by the blood of a goat, so the blood of Christ softens the hardest heart. He takes the whirlwind for the fierceness of the wrath seen in the dispersion.

Clarke reads the withdrawn shoulder of a beast pulling away from under the yoke of the law, restive in the plough, thinks the hard stone may be granite or the mineral of which emery is a species and reports a scholar's view that it was used for polishing others, and refers the whirlwind to the swift victories and cruel conduct of the Chaldeans. Wesley says the same of the shoulder more briefly and supplies the two words that close the chapter, that the people laid the pleasant land desolate by their sins.

Henry catches a different motion in the Hebrew, which he says gives a withdrawing shoulder, so that they seemed to lay it to the work and then drew it back; he keeps two images at once for the hard heart, the diamond hardest to work upon and the flint no mason can hew into shape; he sets the catalogue of refusals in order as one temper rather than four faults; and he draws out the exchange of the following verse, that as they turned a deaf ear to the word in prosperity, so God turned a deaf ear to their prayers in trouble.

debates.question: What is the withdrawn shoulder a figure of?

positions.position: A beast pulling away from under the yoke of the law, restive in the plough.
Not a pulling away at all but the offering of a stubborn shoulder, as an ox refusing the yoke.
A withdrawing shoulder: laid to the work and then drawn back again.
Perhaps granite, or the mineral of which emery is a species, or a stone used for polishing others.
Simply a very hard stone; the word is the ancestor of diamond and was first applied to steel.
Not a stone at all but a creature the size of a barley corn that cuts the hardest stones.
Two images together, the diamond hardest to work upon and the flint no mason can shape.

outliers.claim: The land was left so empty that not a man, woman or child remained and the very roads through it were deserted, in which he finds a hidden mercy, since it was kept empty against their return.
